claim: Complete genetic deficiency for the COPII component SEC24A is compatible with normal survival and development in the mouse.
source: We now report that complete genetic deficiency for the COPII component SEC24A is compatible with normal survival and development in the mouse, despite the fundamental role of SEC24 in COPII vesicle formation and cargo recruitment.
evidence: Demonstrated through generation and characterization of SEC24A-deficient mice showing normal survival, development, and fertility.

claim: SEC24A-deficient mice exhibit markedly reduced plasma cholesterol.
source: However, these animals exhibit markedly reduced plasma cholesterol, with mutations in Apoe and Ldlr epistatic to Sec24a, suggesting a receptor-mediated lipoprotein clearance mechanism.
evidence: Measured plasma cholesterol levels in SEC24A-deficient mice compared to wild-type controls.

claim: Mutations in Apoe and Ldlr are epistatic to Sec24a.
source: However, these animals exhibit markedly reduced plasma cholesterol, with mutations in Apoe and Ldlr epistatic to Sec24a, suggesting a receptor-mediated lipoprotein clearance mechanism.
evidence: Genetic crosses showing that Apoe-/-Sec24agt/gt and Ldlr-/-Sec24agt/gt mice have cholesterol levels indistinguishable from Apoe-/- and Ldlr-/- mice alone.

claim: SEC24A deficiency affects cholesterol metabolism through a receptor-mediated lipoprotein clearance mechanism.
source: However, these animals exhibit markedly reduced plasma cholesterol, with mutations in Apoe and Ldlr epistatic to Sec24a, suggesting a receptor-mediated lipoprotein clearance mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from epistasis experiments with Apoe and Ldlr mutations.

claim: Hepatic LDLR levels are up-regulated in SEC24A-deficient cells.
source: Consistent with these data, hepatic LDLR levels are up-regulated in SEC24A-deficient cells as a consequence of specific dependence of PCSK9, a negative regulator of LDLR, on SEC24A for efficient exit from the ER.
evidence: Immunoblotting demonstrated elevated LDLR levels in liver protein extracts from Sec24agt/gt mice.

claim: PCSK9 depends on SEC24A for efficient exit from the ER.
source: Consistent with these data, hepatic LDLR levels are up-regulated in SEC24A-deficient cells as a consequence of specific dependence of PCSK9, a negative regulator of LDLR, on SEC24A for efficient exit from the ER.
evidence: PCSK9 accumulates in the ER of SEC24A-deficient mice and shows reduced secretion.

claim: PCSK9 is a negative regulator of LDLR.
source: Consistent with these data, hepatic LDLR levels are up-regulated in SEC24A-deficient cells as a consequence of specific dependence of PCSK9, a negative regulator of LDLR, on SEC24A for efficient exit from the ER.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the manuscript.

claim: There is partial overlap in cargo selectivity between SEC24A and SEC24B.
source: Our findings also identify partial overlap in cargo selectivity between SEC24A and SEC24B, suggesting a previously unappreciated heterogeneity in the recruitment of secretory proteins to the COPII vesicles that extends to soluble as well as trans-membrane cargoes.
evidence: Genetic crosses and in vitro budding assays showing SEC24B can partially compensate for SEC24A in PCSK9 secretion.

claim: Heterogeneity in the recruitment of secretory proteins to COPII vesicles extends to soluble as well as trans-membrane cargoes.
source: Our findings also identify partial overlap in cargo selectivity between SEC24A and SEC24B, suggesting a previously unappreciated heterogeneity in the recruitment of secretory proteins to the COPII vesicles that extends to soluble as well as trans-membrane cargoes.
evidence: PCSK9, a soluble cargo, shows specific dependence on SEC24A/B for ER exit.

claim: One-third of the vertebrate genome is predicted to encode proteins that are sorted into the secretory pathway.
source: One-third of the vertebrate genome is predicted to encode proteins that are sorted into the secretory pathway en route to intracellular organelles, the cell surface, or the extracellular space (Palade, 1975; Bonifacino and Glick, 2004).

claim: Trans-membrane and soluble proteins co-translationally inserted into the ER are packaged into transport vesicles coated with COPII for export from the ER and delivery to the Golgi.
source: Following synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum, trans-membrane and soluble proteins co-translationally inserted into the ER are packaged into transport vesicles coated with COPII (coat protein complex II) for export from the ER and delivery to the Golgi for further processing (Lee et al., 2004).

claim: The assembly of the COPII coat is initiated at ER exit sites upon activation of the GTPase SAR1.
source: The assembly of the COPII coat is initiated at ER exit sites upon activation of the GTPase SAR1, which recruits the inner-coat heterodimer SEC23/SEC24, followed by the assembly of the outer-coat heterotetramer SEC13/SEC31 to generate carrier vesicles destined for the Golgi (Lee et al., 2004; Gurkan et al., 2006).

claim: SAR1 recruits the inner-coat heterodimer SEC23/SEC24.
source: The assembly of the COPII coat is initiated at ER exit sites upon activation of the GTPase SAR1, which recruits the inner-coat heterodimer SEC23/SEC24, followed by the assembly of the outer-coat heterotetramer SEC13/SEC31 to generate carrier vesicles destined for the Golgi (Lee et al., 2004; Gurkan et al., 2006).

claim: The SEC24 subunit of the COPII complex recognizes specific signals within cargo molecules.
source: A key sorting event in ER-Golgi transport relies on recognition of specific signals within cargo molecules by the SEC24 subunit of the COPII complex (Miller et al., 2002, 2003; Lee et al., 2004), though SEC23 may also contribute to cargo selection in some cases (Kim et al., 2012).

claim: SEC23 may also contribute to cargo selection in some cases.
source: A key sorting event in ER-Golgi transport relies on recognition of specific signals within cargo molecules by the SEC24 subunit of the COPII complex (Miller et al., 2002, 2003; Lee et al., 2004), though SEC23 may also contribute to cargo selection in some cases (Kim et al., 2012).

claim: The SEC31/SEC13 outer-coat regulates the size and rigidity of COPII coats to package specialized cargos.
source: The SEC31/SEC13 outer-coat regulates the size and rigidity of COPII coats to package specialized cargos (Copic et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2012).

claim: Mammals express multiple paralogous forms of COPII, including two SAR1 GTPases (SAR1A/B), two SEC23s (SEC23A/B), four SEC24s (SEC24A-D), as well as two SEC31s (SEC31A/B).
source: Mammals express multiple paralogous forms of COPII, including two SAR1 GTPases (SAR1A/B), two SEC23s (SEC23A/B), four SEC24s (SEC24A-D), as well as two SEC31s (SEC31A/B), thus expanding the repertoire of potential COPII coat structures (Wendeler et al., 2007; Zanetti et al., 2011).

claim: The four mammalian SEC24 paralogs can be divided into two subfamilies, SEC24A/B and SEC24C/D, sharing ∼60% sequence identity within but only ∼25% identity across subfamilies.
source: The four mammalian SEC24 paralogs can be divided into two subfamilies, SEC24A/B and SEC24C/D, sharing ∼60% sequence identity within but only ∼25% identity across subfamilies (Mancias and Goldberg, 2008; Zanetti et al., 2011).

claim: Mammalian SEC24A/B exhibit ∼30% sequence identity to yeast SEC24p, compared to ∼25% for SEC24C/D.
source: Mammalian SEC24A/B exhibit ∼30% sequence identity to yeast SEC24p, compared to ∼25% for SEC24C/D.

claim: SEC24C/D share ∼30% identity with LST1p or ISS1p, the non-essential SEC24 paralogs in yeast.
source: The latter share ∼30% identity with LST1p or ISS1p, the non-essential SEC24 paralogs in yeast (Roberg et al., 1999; Peng et al., 2000; Shimoni et al., 2000).

claim: Deletions of SAR1, SEC23, or SEC24 are all lethal in yeast.
source: Although deletions of SAR1, SEC23, or SEC24 are all lethal in yeast (Lee et al., 2004), consistent with the broad function of ER-Golgi transport, mutations in the genes encoding several mammalian COPII components have been associated with remarkably limited phenotypes, often restricted to a specific cell type or tissue.

claim: Mutations in the genes encoding several mammalian COPII components have been associated with remarkably limited phenotypes, often restricted to a specific cell type or tissue.
source: Although deletions of SAR1, SEC23, or SEC24 are all lethal in yeast (Lee et al., 2004), consistent with the broad function of ER-Golgi transport, mutations in the genes encoding several mammalian COPII components have been associated with remarkably limited phenotypes, often restricted to a specific cell type or tissue.
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature and examples provided in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in human SAR1B result in chylomicron retention disease (Anderson Disease).
source: Mutations in human SAR1B result in chylomicron retention disease (Anderson Disease), a distinct defect in fat absorption due to reduced chylomicron assembly and secretion by intestinal enterocytes (Jones et al., 2003; Annesi et al., 2007).

claim: Chylomicron retention disease is a distinct defect in fat absorption due to reduced chylomicron assembly and secretion by intestinal enterocytes.
source: Mutations in human SAR1B result in chylomicron retention disease (Anderson Disease), a distinct defect in fat absorption due to reduced chylomicron assembly and secretion by intestinal enterocytes (Jones et al., 2003; Annesi et al., 2007).

claim: Missense mutations in human SEC23A result in a characteristic syndrome of malformations restricted to the craniofacial skeleton.
source: In contrast, missense mutations in human SEC23A result in a characteristic syndrome of malformations restricted to the craniofacial skeleton (Boyadjiev et al., 2006, 2010), with similar skeletal abnormalities observed in SEC23A-deficient zebrafish (Lang et al., 2006).

claim: Similar skeletal abnormalities are observed in SEC23A-deficient zebrafish.
source: In contrast, missense mutations in human SEC23A result in a characteristic syndrome of malformations restricted to the craniofacial skeleton (Boyadjiev et al., 2006, 2010), with similar skeletal abnormalities observed in SEC23A-deficient zebrafish (Lang et al., 2006).

claim: Mutations in human SEC23B result in the autosomal recessive disorder congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II.
source: Mutations in human SEC23B result in the autosomal recessive disorder congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II, with abnormalities restricted to the hematopoietic erythroid compartment (Bianchi et al., 2009; Schwarz et al., 2009).

claim: Red blood cells appear grossly normal in SEC23B-deficient mice.
source: Surprisingly, although red blood cells appear grossly normal in SEC23B-deficient mice, these animals die at birth due to dramatic destruction of the pancreas (Tao et al., 2012).

claim: SEC23B-deficient mice die at birth due to dramatic destruction of the pancreas.
source: Surprisingly, although red blood cells appear grossly normal in SEC23B-deficient mice, these animals die at birth due to dramatic destruction of the pancreas (Tao et al., 2012).

claim: SEC24B deficiency in mice leads to failure in neural tube closure resulting from missorting of the signaling molecule VANGL2.
source: Though human deficiency has not yet been reported for any of the four SEC24 paralogs, SEC24B deficiency in mice leads to failure in neural tube closure resulting from missorting of the signaling molecule VANGL2 (Merte et al., 2010).

claim: Murine SEC24D deficiency results in very early embryonic lethality.
source: In contrast, murine SEC24D deficiency results in very early embryonic lethality (Baines et al., In press).

claim: SEC24A-deficient mice were generated from an ES cell line carrying a gene trap insertion into intron two of Sec24a.
source: SEC24A-deficient mice were generated from an ES cell line carrying a gene trap insertion into intron two of Sec24a (Figure 1A).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The gene trap allele (Sec24agt) is predicted to direct expression of a hybrid mRNA fusing Sec24a exons 1 and 2 with the gene trap cassette, resulting in a chimeric protein missing the C-terminal ∼85% of SEC24A.
source: The gene trap allele (Sec24agt) is predicted to direct expression of a hybrid mRNA fusing Sec24a exons 1 and 2 with the gene trap cassette, resulting in a chimeric protein missing the C-terminal ∼85% of SEC24A (encoded by exons 3–23).
evidence: Predicted based on gene trap design.

claim: An intercross between Sec24a+/gt heterozygous mice produced offspring of all three genotypes at the expected Mendelian ratios.
source: An intercross between Sec24a+/gt heterozygous mice produced offspring of all three genotypes at the expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1).

claim: RT-PCR analysis of liver RNA from Sec24agt/gt mice showed a >1000 fold reduction in normal splicing from Sec24a exon 2 to exon 3 across the gene trap.
source: RT-PCR analysis of liver RNA prepared from Sec24agt/gt mice showed a >1000 fold reduction in normal splicing from Sec24a exon 2 to exon 3 across the gene trap, compared to control wild type mice (Figure 1B).

claim: Immunoblotting detected an ∼50% reduction in SEC24A protein in whole brain protein extracts from heterozygous Sec24a+/gt mice compared to wild type littermates.
source: Immunoblotting detected an ∼50% reduction in SEC24A protein in whole brain protein extracts from heterozygous Sec24a+/gt mice compared to wild type littermates, with no SEC24A detected in extracts from Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 1C).

claim: No SEC24A was detected in extracts from Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: Immunoblotting detected an ∼50% reduction in SEC24A protein in whole brain protein extracts from heterozygous Sec24a+/gt mice compared to wild type littermates, with no SEC24A detected in extracts from Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 1C).

claim: SEC24B protein levels were increased in brain lysates from Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: Of note, SEC24B protein levels were increased in brain lysates from Sec24agt/gt mice, with a potential slight increase in Sec24a+/gt heterozygous mice, though no differences were observed for SEC24C or SEC24D (Figure 1C).

claim: No differences were observed for SEC24C or SEC24D protein levels in brain lysates from Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: Of note, SEC24B protein levels were increased in brain lysates from Sec24agt/gt mice, with a potential slight increase in Sec24a+/gt heterozygous mice, though no differences were observed for SEC24C or SEC24D (Figure 1C).

claim: Sec24agt/gt mice were grossly indistinguishable from their wild type littermates and developed normally to adulthood with no difference in body weight on a normal or high fat diet.
source: Sec24agt/gt mice were grossly indistinguishable from their wild type littermates and developed normally to adulthood with no difference in body weight on a normal or high fat diet (Figure 1D).
evidence: Body weight measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Kaplan-Meier analysis showed no difference in the survival of wild type and Sec24agt/gt mice up to 12 months of age.
source: Kaplan-Meier analysis showed no difference in the survival of wild type and Sec24agt/gt mice up to 12 months of age (Figure 1E).

claim: Sec24agt/gt male and female mice both exhibited normal fertility at ∼8 weeks of age with normal litter size.
source: Sec24agt/gt male and female mice both exhibited normal fertility at ∼8 weeks of age with normal litter size (7.7 ± 1.4, n = 6, compared to 7.1 ± 1.0, n = 10 for congenic C57BL6/J controls, p>0.35).

claim: Gross and routine microscopic survey of multiple tissues failed to identify any obvious morphologic abnormalities in adult Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: Gross and routine microscopic survey of multiple tissues failed to identify any obvious morphologic abnormalities in adult Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 1F).

claim: Complete blood count surveys were essentially normal in Sec24agt/gt mice compared to wild type controls, except for an ∼4% increase in mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and a compensatory ∼6% decrease in red blood cell (RBC) number.
source: Complete blood count (CBC) surveys were essentially normal in Sec24agt/gt mice compared to wild type controls, except for an ∼4% increase in mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and a compensatory ∼6% decrease in red blood cell (RBC) number (Table 2).

claim: An additional series of Sec24a deficient mice were generated from a second, independent Sec24a targeted allele.
source: To exclude a contribution from residual function of the Sec24agt allele or a potential 'passenger' gene mutation as a result of gene targeting (Westrick et al., 2010), we generated an additional series of Sec24a deficient mice from a second, independent Sec24a targeted allele (Figure 2A).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sec24a+/cgt or Sec24a+/gt2 intercrosses both produced offspring with all three genotypes at the expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Sec24a+/cgt or Sec24a+/gt2 intercrosses both produced offspring with all three genotypes at the expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1).

claim: No SEC24A protein was detected in brain protein extracts from either Sec24acgt/cgt or Sec24agt2/gt2 mice.
source: No SEC24A protein was detected in brain protein extracts from either Sec24acgt/cgt or Sec24agt2/gt2 mice (Figure 2B).

claim: SEC24A is not required for survival, development, or fertility in the mouse.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrated that SEC24A is not required for survival, development, or fertility in the mouse.
evidence: Multiple independent SEC24A-deficient mouse lines show normal survival, development, and fertility.

claim: SDS-PAGE analysis of non-reduced plasma samples from Sec24agt/gt mice and their wild type littermates demonstrated no changes in several abundant plasma proteins, including albumin and transferrin.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of non-reduced plasma samples from Sec24agt/gt mice and their wild type littermates demonstrated no changes in several abundant plasma proteins, including albumin and transferrin (Figure 3A asterisks).

claim: A protein migrating at ∼25 kD consistently appeared under-represented by ∼50% in plasma samples from Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: However, a protein migrating at ∼25 kD consistently appeared under-represented by ∼50% in plasma samples from Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 3A arrow, p25).
evidence: SDS-PAGE gel and quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified the ∼25 kD protein as apolipoprotein A-I (APO-A1).
source: Mass spectrometry identified this protein as apolipoprotein A-I (APO-A1) (Figure 3B), and quantification by spectral counts or mean peak area confirmed an ∼30–70% reduction of APO-A1 in Sec24agt/gt plasma compared to wild type.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Quantification by spectral counts or mean peak area confirmed an ∼30–70% reduction of APO-A1 in Sec24agt/gt plasma compared to wild type.
source: Mass spectrometry identified this protein as apolipoprotein A-I (APO-A1) (Figure 3B), and quantification by spectral counts or mean peak area confirmed an ∼30–70% reduction of APO-A1 in Sec24agt/gt plasma compared to wild type.

claim: Immunoblotting confirmed an ∼40% decrease in APO-A1 levels in Sec24agt/gt plasma.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed an ∼40% decrease in APO-A1 levels in Sec24agt/gt plasma (Figure 3C).

claim: APO-A1 is a core protein component of high-density cholesterol-containing lipoprotein particles.
source: APO-A1 is a core protein component of high-density cholesterol-containing lipoprotein particles and is also found in some other lipoprotein particle species in the circulation (Hoofnagle and Heinecke, 2009).

claim: Total cholesterol and High Density Lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol were reduced by ∼40% in Sec24agt/gt plasma compared to wild type.
source: Total cholesterol and High Density Lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol were reduced by ∼40% in Sec24agt/gt plasma compared to wild type, and Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol by ∼60%.
evidence: FPLC fractionation and cholesterol quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol was reduced by ∼60% in Sec24agt/gt plasma compared to wild type.
source: Total cholesterol and High Density Lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol were reduced by ∼40% in Sec24agt/gt plasma compared to wild type, and Low Density Lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol by ∼60%.
evidence: FPLC fractionation and cholesterol quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reduced plasma cholesterol levels were observed in both male and female SEC24A-deficient mice at different ages.
source: Similarly reduced plasma cholesterol levels were observed in both male and female SEC24A-deficient mice at different ages (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Cholesterol measurements shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: The low cholesterol phenotype was confirmed in mice harboring the second SEC24A-deficient allele, Sec24agt2/gt2.
source: The low cholesterol phenotype was also confirmed in mice harboring the second SEC24A-deficient allele, Sec24agt2/gt2 (Figure 3G).

claim: Removal of the conditional gene trap cassette from the Sec24acgt allele by germline Flpe-mediated excision generated the Sec24afl allele.
source: To further exclude a potential contribution from a passenger gene to the hypocholesterolemia phenotype (Westrick et al., 2010), we removed the conditional gene trap cassette from the Sec24acgt allele by germline Flpe-mediated excision (see Experimental procedures) to generate the Sec24afl allele.

claim: Sec24afl/fl mice exhibited full restoration of SEC24A expression in liver lysates.
source: Sec24afl/fl mice exhibited full restoration of SEC24A expression in liver lysates (Figure 4A), as well as normalization of total plasma cholesterol levels (Figure 4B).

claim: Sec24afl/fl mice exhibited normalization of total plasma cholesterol levels.
source: Sec24afl/fl mice exhibited full restoration of SEC24A expression in liver lysates (Figure 4A), as well as normalization of total plasma cholesterol levels (Figure 4B).

claim: Sec24a is ubiquitously expressed in multiple tissues.
source: Analysis of public mRNA expression data revealed that Sec24a is ubiquitously expressed in multiple tissues (Rosenbloom et al., 2012).
evidence: Referenced from public mRNA expression data.

claim: SEC24A was present in all tissues tested, although it was relatively enriched in the liver.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed that SEC24A was present in all tissues tested, although it was relatively enriched in the liver (Figure 4C).

claim: Expression of SEC24A was reduced by 70–80% in the liver of Adv-Cre-treated Sec24afl/fl mice.
source: Expression of SEC24A was reduced by 70–80% in the liver of Adv-Cre-treated Sec24afl/fl mice (Figure 4D), resulting in an ∼25% decrease in total cholesterol levels compared to wild type control mice receiving the same adenovirus (Figure 4E).

claim: Hepatic inactivation of SEC24A resulted in an ∼25% decrease in total cholesterol levels compared to wild type control mice.
source: Expression of SEC24A was reduced by 70–80% in the liver of Adv-Cre-treated Sec24afl/fl mice (Figure 4D), resulting in an ∼25% decrease in total cholesterol levels compared to wild type control mice receiving the same adenovirus (Figure 4E).

claim: Loss of hepatic Sec24a expression is sufficient to explain the hypocholesterolemia observed in SEC24A-deficient mice.
source: Although this reduction in plasma cholesterol was less than observed in Sec24agt/gt mice, considering the incomplete deletion of hepatic Sec24a by Adv-Cre, these data suggest that loss of hepatic Sec24a expression is sufficient to explain the hypocholesterolemia observed in SEC24A-deficient mice.
evidence: Hepatic-specific deletion of SEC24A reduces plasma cholesterol.

claim: The SREBP1/2 transcription factors are key determinants of cholesterol metabolism.
source: The SREBP1/2 transcription factors, key determinants of cholesterol metabolism (Brown and Goldstein, 1997, 2009), undergo cleavage-dependent activation at the Golgi apparatus regulated by COPII-mediated transport from the ER through the chaperone protein SCAP (Sun et al., 2005, 2007; Brown and Goldstein, 2009).

claim: SREBP1/2 undergo cleavage-dependent activation at the Golgi apparatus regulated by COPII-mediated transport from the ER through the chaperone protein SCAP.
source: The SREBP1/2 transcription factors, key determinants of cholesterol metabolism (Brown and Goldstein, 1997, 2009), undergo cleavage-dependent activation at the Golgi apparatus regulated by COPII-mediated transport from the ER through the chaperone protein SCAP (Sun et al., 2005, 2007; Brown and Goldstein, 2009).

claim: No significant differences were observed in the expression levels of the 20 most abundant hepatic transcripts between wild type and Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: No significant differences were observed in the expression levels of the 20 most abundant hepatic transcripts between wild type and Sec24agt/gt mice (<1.2 fold, False Discovery Rate [FDR] > 0.4, Figure 5B).

claim: Among the ∼20,000 identified transcripts, only ∼30 showed significant down-regulation (>2 fold, FDR < 0.05, RPKM > 0.2).
source: Among the ∼20,000 identified transcripts, only ∼30 showed significant down-regulation (>2 fold, FDR < 0.05, RPKM > 0.2), with Sec24a as the most significantly down-regulated mRNA in Sec24agt/gt liver (Figure 5C).

claim: Sec24a was the most significantly down-regulated mRNA in Sec24agt/gt liver.
source: Among the ∼20,000 identified transcripts, only ∼30 showed significant down-regulation (>2 fold, FDR < 0.05, RPKM > 0.2), with Sec24a as the most significantly down-regulated mRNA in Sec24agt/gt liver (Figure 5C).

claim: Gene-ontology enrichment analysis failed to identify a consistent pattern in the changes in transcript levels.
source: Gene-ontology enrichment analysis failed to identify a consistent pattern in the changes in transcript levels, though modest shifts were noted in a few metabolic genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of mRNA-Seq data.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the gene expression profile for Sec24agt/gt mice and previously reported profiles from mice with altered expression of SCAP or SREBP1/2.
source: There was no significant correlation between the gene expression profile for Sec24agt/gt mice and previously reported profiles from mice with altered expression of SCAP or SREBP1/2 (Horton et al., 2003).

claim: Transcripts for direct SREBP1/2 targets, including the Low Density Lipoprotein Receptor (LDLR), HMG-CoA reductase, and PCSK9, remained unchanged by mRNA-seq and qPCR.
source: Specifically, transcripts for direct SREBP1/2 targets, including the Low Density Lipoprotein Receptor (LDLR), HMG-CoA reductase, and PCSK9, remained unchanged by mRNA-seq and qPCR, though SCD1 was decreased by ∼50% in Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 5D), as observed by mRNA-seq (FDR < 3 × 10−13).
evidence: mRNA-Seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SCD1 was decreased by ∼50% in Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: Specifically, transcripts for direct SREBP1/2 targets, including the Low Density Lipoprotein Receptor (LDLR), HMG-CoA reductase, and PCSK9, remained unchanged by mRNA-seq and qPCR, though SCD1 was decreased by ∼50% in Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 5D), as observed by mRNA-seq (FDR < 3 × 10−13).
evidence: mRNA-Seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No detectable difference in the extent of SREBP1/2 cleavage was observed by immunoblotting of liver lysates from Sec24agt/gt mice and their wild type littermates.
source: In addition, no detectable difference in the extent of SREBP1/2 cleavage was observed by immunoblotting of liver lysates from Sec24agt/gt mice and their wild type littermates (Figure 5E).

claim: RNA-seq detected expression of all four SEC24 paralogs in normal liver.
source: Of note, RNA-seq detected expression of all four SEC24 paralogs in normal liver, with the number of transcripts for Sec24c and Sec24d–twofold greater than Sec24a and 5–10 fold greater than Sec24b (Figure 5F).

claim: The number of transcripts for Sec24c and Sec24d was twofold greater than Sec24a and 5–10 fold greater than Sec24b in normal liver.
source: Of note, RNA-seq detected expression of all four SEC24 paralogs in normal liver, with the number of transcripts for Sec24c and Sec24d–twofold greater than Sec24a and 5–10 fold greater than Sec24b (Figure 5F).

claim: Quantitative immunoblotting confirmed the presence of SEC24C/D proteins at similar levels to SEC24A in wild type liver.
source: Quantitative immunoblotting using RFP-tagged SEC24A and SEC24C/D as references confirmed the presence of SEC24C/D proteins at similar levels to SEC24A in wild type liver, and no change in SEC24C/D levels in Sec24agt/gt liver (Figure 5G).

claim: There was no change in SEC24C/D levels in Sec24agt/gt liver.
source: Quantitative immunoblotting using RFP-tagged SEC24A and SEC24C/D as references confirmed the presence of SEC24C/D proteins at similar levels to SEC24A in wild type liver, and no change in SEC24C/D levels in Sec24agt/gt liver (Figure 5G).

claim: Apoe-/- mice showed markedly elevated cholesterol levels (272 ± 13 mg/dl, n = 8).
source: Consistent with previous reports (Piedrahita et al., 1992; Zhang et al., 1992), Apoe-/- mice showed markedly elevated cholesterol levels (272 ± 13 mg/dl, n = 8).

claim: The plasma cholesterol levels in Apoe-/-Sec24agt/gt mice (277 ± 14 mg/dl, n = 7) were indistinguishable (p>0.8) from singly Apoe-/- littermates.
source: However, in contrast to the ∼45% reduction in plasma cholesterol observed in mice singly deficient for Sec24a (Figure 3D), the plasma cholesterol levels in Apoe-/-Sec24agt/gt mice (277 ± 14 mg/dl, n = 7) were indistinguishable (p>0.8) from singly Apoe-/- littermates (Figure 6A).

claim: Ldlr-/- mice exhibited markedly elevated plasma cholesterol levels (211 ± 9 mg/dl, n = 14).
source: Consistent with previous reports (Ishibashi et al., 1993), Ldlr-/- mice exhibited markedly elevated plasma cholesterol levels (211 ± 9 mg/dl, n = 14).

claim: Doubly deficient Ldlr-/-Sec24agt/gt mice displayed similarly elevated plasma cholesterol levels (197 ± 12 mg/dl, n = 11), indistinguishable (p>0.35) from their Ldlr-/- littermates.
source: Doubly deficient Ldlr-/-Sec24agt/gt mice also displayed similarly elevated plasma cholesterol levels (197 ± 12 mg/dl, n = 11), indistinguishable (p>0.35) from their Ldlr-/- littermates (Figure 6B).

claim: Reduction in plasma cholesterol in SEC24A-deficient mice results from increased clearance of cholesterol-rich lipoproteins by the LDLR.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that reduction in plasma cholesterol in SEC24A-deficient mice could result from increased clearance of cholesterol-rich lipoproteins by the LDLR.
evidence: Inferred from epistasis experiments with Apoe and Ldlr mutations.

claim: Immunoblotting demonstrated elevated LDLR levels in liver protein extracts from Sec24agt/gt mice compared to littermate controls.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, immunoblotting demonstrated elevated LDLR levels in liver protein extracts or in proteins bound to a wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) matrix from Sec24agt/gt mice compared to littermate controls, whereas other proteins including APOE, APOB48/100, or APO-A1 showed little alteration in the liver (Figure 6C).

claim: Other proteins including APOE, APOB48/100, or APO-A1 showed little alteration in the liver of Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, immunoblotting demonstrated elevated LDLR levels in liver protein extracts or in proteins bound to a wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) matrix from Sec24agt/gt mice compared to littermate controls, whereas other proteins including APOE, APOB48/100, or APO-A1 showed little alteration in the liver (Figure 6C).

claim: Hepatic Ldlr transcripts remained unaltered in Sec24agt/gt by both mRNA-Seq and qPCR.
source: Since hepatic Ldlr transcripts remained unaltered in Sec24agt/gt by both mRNA-Seq and qPCR (Figure 5D), these data indicate that the reduction in LDLR protein levels in SEC24A-deficient mice was mediated via a translational or post-translational mechanism.
evidence: mRNA-Seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The increase in LDLR protein levels in SEC24A-deficient mice was mediated via a translational or post-translational mechanism.
source: Since hepatic Ldlr transcripts remained unaltered in Sec24agt/gt by both mRNA-Seq and qPCR (Figure 5D), these data indicate that the reduction in LDLR protein levels in SEC24A-deficient mice was mediated via a translational or post-translational mechanism.
evidence: LDLR protein levels are increased while mRNA levels remain unchanged.

claim: LDLR levels are regulated by intracellular factors such as the E3 ligase IDOL and circulating PCSK9.
source: LDLR levels are regulated by intracellular factors such as the E3 ligase IDOL (Zelcer et al., 2009) and circulating PCSK9.

claim: PCSK9 is secreted into the plasma primarily by hepatocytes, binding to LDLR and promoting its endocytosis and degradation.
source: The latter is secreted into the plasma primarily by hepatocytes, binding to LDLR and promoting its endocytosis and degradation (Costet et al., 2008; Horton et al., 2009).

claim: No difference in the level of IDOL was observed in immunoblotting of liver lysates prepared from SEC24A-deficient mice compared to their wild type littermates.
source: No difference in the level of IDOL was observed in immunoblotting of liver lysates prepared from SEC24A-deficient mice compared to their wild type littermates (Figure 6C).

claim: An ∼55% reduction of plasma PCSK9 was observed in Sec24agt/gt mice.
source: To assess a potential role for PCSK9 in the low plasma cholesterol phenotype of SEC24A-deficient mice, we measured circulating PCSK9 levels by ELISA. An ∼55% reduction of plasma PCSK9 was observed in Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 6D), suggesting that SEC24A-deficiency may lower plasma cholesterol via reduced secretion of PCSK9.

claim: SEC24A-deficiency may lower plasma cholesterol via reduced secretion of PCSK9.
source: To assess a potential role for PCSK9 in the low plasma cholesterol phenotype of SEC24A-deficient mice, we measured circulating PCSK9 levels by ELISA. An ∼55% reduction of plasma PCSK9 was observed in Sec24agt/gt mice (Figure 6D), suggesting that SEC24A-deficiency may lower plasma cholesterol via reduced secretion of PCSK9.
evidence: Reduced plasma PCSK9 levels in SEC24A-deficient mice.

claim: No change in PCSK9 hepatic mRNA was observed between SEC24agt/gt mice and their wild type littermates by mRNA-seq or qPCR.
source: No change in PCSK9 hepatic mRNA was observed between SEC24agt/gt mice and their wild type littermates by mRNA-seq or qPCR (Figure 5D), suggesting a translational or post-translational mechanism for the reduction of circulating PCSK9 in SEC24A-deficient mice.
evidence: mRNA-Seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The reduction of circulating PCSK9 in SEC24A-deficient mice occurs via a translational or post-translational mechanism.
source: No change in PCSK9 hepatic mRNA was observed between SEC24agt/gt mice and their wild type littermates by mRNA-seq or qPCR (Figure 5D), suggesting a translational or post-translational mechanism for the reduction of circulating PCSK9 in SEC24A-deficient mice.
evidence: PCSK9 protein levels are reduced while mRNA levels remain unchanged.

claim: Analysis of liver protein extracts by immunoblotting demonstrated significant accumulation of both mature and pro-PCSK9 in the liver of Sec24agt/gt mice compared to littermate controls.
source: Analysis of liver protein extracts by immunoblotting demonstrated significant accumulation of both mature and pro-PCSK9 in the liver of Sec24agt/gt mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 7A).

claim: Nearly all of the intracellularly-accumulated PCSK9 in Sec24agt/gt liver exhibited sensitivity to EndoH.
source: To determine the site of PCSK9 intracellular accumulation, we treated liver lysates with endoglycosidase H (EndoH). Nearly all of the intracellularly-accumulated PCSK9 in Sec24agt/gt liver exhibited sensitivity to EndoH with faster eletrophoresis mobility (Figure 7B), suggesting that SEC24A deficiency leads to accumulation of PCSK9 in the ER.
evidence: EndoH treatment data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SEC24A deficiency leads to accumulation of PCSK9 in the ER.
source: To determine the site of PCSK9 intracellular accumulation, we treated liver lysates with endoglycosidase H (EndoH). Nearly all of the intracellularly-accumulated PCSK9 in Sec24agt/gt liver exhibited sensitivity to EndoH with faster eletrophoresis mobility (Figure 7B), suggesting that SEC24A deficiency leads to accumulation of PCSK9 in the ER.

claim: COPII-dependent ER-Golgi transport plays a critical role in PCSK9 secretion from the cell.
source: These data suggest that COPII-dependent ER-Golgi transport plays a critical role in PCSK9 secretion from the cell.
evidence: PCSK9 accumulates in the ER and secretion is blocked by BFA and dominant-negative SAR1.

claim: When BFA was applied to a 293T cell line stably expressing PCSK9-FLAG, PCSK9 secretion into the medium was abolished and the protein accumulated intracellularly.
source: Belfeldin A (BFA) disrupts the Golgi apparatus and consequently the delivery of ER-derived COPII vesicles along the secretory pathway. When BFA was applied to a 293T cell line stably expressing PCSK9 fused with a C-terminal FLAG tag (PCSK9-FLAG), PCSK9 secretion into the medium was abolished and the protein accumulated intracellularly (Figure 7C).
evidence: BFA treatment data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the presence of rat liver cytosol supplying COPII components, along with ATP and GTP, PCSK9 was packaged into COPII vesicles.
source: To directly test whether the COPII machinery plays a role in ER exiting of PCSK9, we employed permeabilized 293T cells stably expressing PCSK9-FLAG in an in vitro COPII vesicle budding assay. In the presence of rat liver cytosol supplying COPII components, along with ATP and GTP, PCSK9 was packaged into COPII vesicles that sedimented in a high-speed pellet fraction, together with the classic COPII cargo SEC22B, but not the ER resident protein roboporin (Figure 7D).
evidence: In vitro COPII budding assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ER budding of PCSK9 and SEC22B-containing vesicles were inhibited by GTPyS as well as constitutively active SAR1 (SAR1A H79G).
source: ER budding of PCSK9 and SEC22B-containing vesicles were inhibited by GTPyS as well as constitutively active SAR1 (SAR1A H79G), both of which prevent GTP hydrolysis and subsequently COPII vesicle budding from the ER membrane (Figure 7D).
evidence: In vitro COPII budding assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Inhibition of COPII vesicle formation in cells by SAR1B H79G prevented secretion of PCSK9 into the medium, with corresponding intracellular accumulation of the protein.
source: Inhibition of COPII vesicle formation in cells by SAR1B H79G also prevented secretion of PCSK9 into the medium, with corresponding intracellular accumulation of the protein (Figure 7E).
evidence: Dominant-negative SAR1 expression data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: PCSK9 secretion is dependent on ER exiting in COPII-coated vesicles.
source: These data demonstrate that PCSK9 secretion is dependent on ER exiting in COPII-coated vesicles.
evidence: Multiple experiments showing PCSK9 packaging into COPII vesicles and inhibition by blocking COPII function.

claim: SEC24A and SEC24B, but not SEC24C or SEC24D, associated with PCSK9 precipitated by anti-FLAG antibody in CHAPS-based buffer.
source: To test whether SEC24 paralogs provide specificity in transporting PCSK9, we introduced RFP-tagged SEC24A-D paired with GFP-tagged SEC23A into 293T cells stably expressing PCSK9-FLAG. SEC24A and SEC24B, but not SEC24C or SEC24D, associated with PCSK9 precipitated by anti-FLAG antibody in CHAPS-based buffer (Figure 8A), suggesting that SEC24A and SEC24B may selectively mediate PCSK9 ER exiting and secretion.

claim: SEC24A and SEC24B may selectively mediate PCSK9 ER exiting and secretion.
source: To test whether SEC24 paralogs provide specificity in transporting PCSK9, we introduced RFP-tagged SEC24A-D paired with GFP-tagged SEC23A into 293T cells stably expressing PCSK9-FLAG. SEC24A and SEC24B, but not SEC24C or SEC24D, associated with PCSK9 precipitated by anti-FLAG antibody in CHAPS-based buffer (Figure 8A), suggesting that SEC24A and SEC24B may selectively mediate PCSK9 ER exiting and secretion.

claim: Expression of SEC24A paired with SEC23A (5.4 ± 1.7 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05) reduced intracellular levels of PCSK9 and led to increased secretion of the protein into the medium.
source: To directly test this hypothesis, we introduced RFP-tagged SEC24A-D paired with GFP-tagged SEC23A together with PCSK9-FLAG into 293T cells. Expression of SEC24A paired with SEC23A (5.4 ± 1.7 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05), and to a lesser extent SEC24B/SEC23A (2.1 ± 0.4 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05), reduced intracellular levels of PCSK9 and led to increased secretion of the protein into the medium, while SEC24C or SEC24D in complex with SEC23A had little effect (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Overexpression and secretion assay data shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: SEC24B/SEC23A (2.1 ± 0.4 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05) reduced intracellular levels of PCSK9 and led to increased secretion of the protein into the medium.
source: To directly test this hypothesis, we introduced RFP-tagged SEC24A-D paired with GFP-tagged SEC23A together with PCSK9-FLAG into 293T cells. Expression of SEC24A paired with SEC23A (5.4 ± 1.7 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05), and to a lesser extent SEC24B/SEC23A (2.1 ± 0.4 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05), reduced intracellular levels of PCSK9 and led to increased secretion of the protein into the medium, while SEC24C or SEC24D in complex with SEC23A had little effect (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Overexpression and secretion assay data shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: SEC24C or SEC24D in complex with SEC23A had little effect on PCSK9 secretion.
source: To directly test this hypothesis, we introduced RFP-tagged SEC24A-D paired with GFP-tagged SEC23A together with PCSK9-FLAG into 293T cells. Expression of SEC24A paired with SEC23A (5.4 ± 1.7 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05), and to a lesser extent SEC24B/SEC23A (2.1 ± 0.4 fold compared to RFP control, p<0.05), reduced intracellular levels of PCSK9 and led to increased secretion of the protein into the medium, while SEC24C or SEC24D in complex with SEC23A had little effect (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Overexpression and secretion assay data shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: The effect of SEC24A/B on PCSK9 secretion was absent when ER-Golgi transport was blocked by BFA treatment.
source: This effect was absent when ER-Golgi transport was blocked by BFA treatment, further suggesting that SEC24A, and to a lesser extent SEC24B, selectively mediate COPII-dependent secretion of PCSK9.
evidence: BFA treatment abolishes the effect of SEC24A/B overexpression on PCSK9 secretion.

claim: PCSK9 packaging into COPII vesicles was reduced upon depletion of SEC24A.
source: To more directly examine the dependence of PCSK9 on SEC24A for efficient exit from the ER, the in vitro COPII vesicle budding assay was performed using cytosols from rat hepatoma McA-RH777 cells treated with control siRNA, or siRNAs against SEC24A, SEC24B, or both proteins. Depletion of SEC24A/B was confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 8D). Compared to control siRNA treatment, PCSK9 packaging into COPII vesicles was reduced upon depletion of SEC24A (Figure 8E,F), and to a greater extent with depletion of both SEC24A and SEC24B.
evidence: In vitro COPII budding assay with siRNA-depleted cytosols shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: PCSK9 packaging into COPII vesicles was reduced to a greater extent with depletion of both SEC24A and SEC24B.
source: To more directly examine the dependence of PCSK9 on SEC24A for efficient exit from the ER, the in vitro COPII vesicle budding assay was performed using cytosols from rat hepatoma McA-RH777 cells treated with control siRNA, or siRNAs against SEC24A, SEC24B, or both proteins. Depletion of SEC24A/B was confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 8D). Compared to control siRNA treatment, PCSK9 packaging into COPII vesicles was reduced upon depletion of SEC24A (Figure 8E,F), and to a greater extent with depletion of both SEC24A and SEC24B.
evidence: In vitro COPII budding assay with siRNA-depleted cytosols shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: Similar reduction in COPII vesicle packing was observed for SEC22B upon depletion of SEC24A/B, consistent with the previous report of its selectivity as a cargo for SEC24A/B.
source: Similar reduction in COPII vesicle packing was observed for SEC22B, consistent with the previous report of its selectivity as a cargo for SEC24A/B (Mancias and Goldberg, 2007).
evidence: In vitro COPII budding assay and cited literature.

claim: Packaging of the non-selective cargo, LMAN1, was not significantly altered by depletion of SEC24A, SEC24B, or both.
source: In contrast, packaging of the non-selective cargo, LMAN1, was not significantly altered by depletion of SEC24A, SEC24B, or both, consistent with previous reports (Mancias and Goldberg, 2007; Wendeler et al., 2007).
evidence: In vitro COPII budding assay and cited literature.

claim: Haplo-deficiency for both Sec24a and Sec24b resulted in no discernible phenotype and normal plasma cholesterol levels.
source: To test the selectivity of SEC24 paralogs in vivo, we performed crosses between SEC24B- and SEC24A-deficient mice (Table 1). Haplo-deficiency for both Sec24a and Sec24b resulted in no discernible phenotype and normal plasma cholesterol levels (Figure 9A).

claim: Sec24agt/gt mice that were also haplo-deficient for Sec24b exhibited a further ∼25% reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to Sec24agt/gt littermates.
source: However, Sec24agt/gt mice that were also haplo-deficient for Sec24b exhibited a further ∼25% reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to Sec24agt/gt littermates (Figure 9A), although they appeared otherwise normal.

claim: There is a partial overlap in function between SEC24A and SEC24B.
source: However, Sec24agt/gt mice that were also haplo-deficient for Sec24b exhibited a further ∼25% reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to Sec24agt/gt littermates (Figure 9A), although they appeared otherwise normal. These data suggest a partial overlap in function between SEC24A and SEC24B.
evidence: Genetic interaction between Sec24a and Sec24b deficiencies.

claim: Sec24a+/gtSec24d+/gt compound heterozygous mice exhibited no discernible phenotype and had normal plasma cholesterol.
source: The possibility of genetic interaction between Sec24a and Sec24d was also examined (Table 1). As for SEC24B above, Sec24a+/gtSec24d+/gt compound heterozygous mice also exhibited no discernible phenotype and had normal plasma cholesterol (Figure 9B).

claim: Sec24agt/gtSec24d+/gt mice were viable.
source: Although SEC24D deficiency in mice results in early embryonic lethality (Baines et al., In press), Sec24agt/gtSec24d+/gt mice were also viable (Table 1) and displayed no further reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to Sec24agt/gt littermates (Figure 9B), indicating distinct functions between SEC24D and SEC24A/B.

claim: Sec24agt/gtSec24d+/gt mice displayed no further reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to Sec24agt/gt littermates.
source: Although SEC24D deficiency in mice results in early embryonic lethality (Baines et al., In press), Sec24agt/gtSec24d+/gt mice were also viable (Table 1) and displayed no further reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to Sec24agt/gt littermates (Figure 9B), indicating distinct functions between SEC24D and SEC24A/B.

claim: There are distinct functions between SEC24D and SEC24A/B.
source: Although SEC24D deficiency in mice results in early embryonic lethality (Baines et al., In press), Sec24agt/gtSec24d+/gt mice were also viable (Table 1) and displayed no further reduction in plasma cholesterol compared to Sec24agt/gt littermates (Figure 9B), indicating distinct functions between SEC24D and SEC24A/B.
evidence: Lack of genetic interaction between Sec24a and Sec24d deficiencies.

claim: The finding that complete deficiency of the COPII subunit SEC24A is compatible with normal survival and development in the mouse is surprising, in light of its ubiquitous expression and presumed fundamental function in the secretory pathway.
source: The finding that complete deficiency of the COPII subunit SEC24A is compatible with normal survival and development in the mouse is surprising, in light of its ubiquitous expression and presumed fundamental function in the secretory pathway.

claim: Examination of SEC24A-deficient animals uncovered an unexpected reduction in plasma cholesterol due to a specific block in the secretion of PCSK9.
source: However, examination of these animals uncovered an unexpected reduction in plasma cholesterol due to a specific block in the secretion of PCSK9, a circulating regulator of cell surface LDL receptor (Costet et al., 2008; Horton et al., 2009).
evidence: Multiple experiments showing reduced plasma cholesterol and PCSK9 secretion in SEC24A-deficient mice.

claim: Genetic crosses demonstrate that both Apoe and Ldlr are epistatic to Sec24a.
source: Genetic crosses demonstrate that both Apoe and Ldlr are epistatic to Sec24a, suggesting that SEC24A primarily affects receptor-mediated cholesterol clearance of cholesterol-rich lipoproteins.
evidence: Epistasis experiments shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: SEC24A primarily affects receptor-mediated cholesterol clearance of cholesterol-rich lipoproteins.
source: Genetic crosses demonstrate that both Apoe and Ldlr are epistatic to Sec24a, suggesting that SEC24A primarily affects receptor-mediated cholesterol clearance of cholesterol-rich lipoproteins.

claim: Yeast SEC24p play a central role in the recruitment of cargo proteins into COPII vesicles to enter the secretory pathway.
source: Yeast SEC24p play a central role in the recruitment of cargo proteins into COPII vesicles to enter the secretory pathway (Miller et al., 2002, 2003), and the non-essential SEC24 homologs LST1p and ISS1p may co-operate with SEC24p for efficient sorting of a specialized set of cargos (Roberg et al., 1999; Peng et al., 2000; Shimoni et al., 2000).

claim: The non-essential SEC24 homologs LST1p and ISS1p may co-operate with SEC24p for efficient sorting of a specialized set of cargos.
source: Yeast SEC24p play a central role in the recruitment of cargo proteins into COPII vesicles to enter the secretory pathway (Miller et al., 2002, 2003), and the non-essential SEC24 homologs LST1p and ISS1p may co-operate with SEC24p for efficient sorting of a specialized set of cargos (Roberg et al., 1999; Peng et al., 2000; Shimoni et al., 2000).

claim: The expansion of the SEC24 family in vertebrates may have facilitated the accommodation of a wider range of cargo proteins.
source: The expansion of the SEC24 family in vertebrates may have facilitated the accommodation of a wider range of cargo proteins (Jensen and Schekman, 2011; Zanetti et al., 2011).

claim: The wide range of SEC24-deficient phenotypes in vertebrates could be explained by either (1) paralog-specific sorting selectivity encoded by intrinsic cargo selectivity or (2) tissue/cell-type-specific differences in relative abundance.
source: This wide range of SEC24-deficient phenotypes in vertebrates could be explained by either (1) paralog-specific sorting selectivity encoded by intrinsic cargo selectivity or (2) tissue/cell-type-specific differences in relative abundance.
evidence: Proposed hypotheses to explain observed phenotypes.

claim: Intrinsic cargo selectivity among SEC24 paralogs is a key determinant of SEC24 function.
source: Our data, together with those of Merte et al. (Merte et al., 2010), suggest that intrinsic cargo selectivity among SEC24 paralogs is a key determinant of SEC24 function.
evidence: Experimental data showing specific cargo dependencies on SEC24 paralogs.

claim: VANGL2 specifically depends on the SEC24B paralog for ER exiting.
source: The latter authors demonstrated specific dependence of VANGL2, a key component of the planar cell polarity signaling pathway, on the SEC24B paralog for ER exiting (Merte et al., 2010).

claim: PCSK9 is a specific SEC24A-dependent COPII cargo.
source: Our findings identify PCSK9 as a specific SEC24A-dependent COPII cargo.
evidence: Multiple experiments showing PCSK9 dependence on SEC24A for ER exit and secretion.

claim: Loss of SEC24A disrupts PCSK9 secretion without affecting other COPII-dependent processes such as SREBP activation.
source: Although all four SEC24 paralogs are expressed in the liver, loss of SEC24A disrupts PCSK9 secretion without affecting other COPII-dependent processes such as SREBP activation.
evidence: SREBP cleavage is normal in SEC24A-deficient mice while PCSK9 secretion is impaired.

claim: SEC24B exhibits limited compensation for SEC24A.
source: SEC24B exhibits limited compensation for SEC24A, with combined genetic deficiencies providing no evidence for functional overlap with SEC24D.
evidence: Genetic crosses showing partial compensation by SEC24B but not SEC24D.

claim: Combined genetic deficiencies provide no evidence for functional overlap between SEC24A and SEC24D.
source: SEC24B exhibits limited compensation for SEC24A, with combined genetic deficiencies providing no evidence for functional overlap with SEC24D.
evidence: Genetic crosses showing no interaction between Sec24a and Sec24d deficiencies.

claim: The data suggest overlapping cargo specificities between the members of the SEC24A/B subfamily, yet distinct from SEC24C/D.
source: These data suggest overlapping cargo specificities between the members of the SEC24A/B subfamily, yet distinct from SEC24C/D.
evidence: Genetic and biochemical experiments showing partial overlap between SEC24A/B but not with SEC24C/D.

claim: Steady state levels of SEC24B, but not SEC24C/D, are increased in the absence of SEC24A.
source: Furthermore, steady state levels of SEC24B, but not SEC24C/D, are increased in the absence of SEC24A (Figure 1C), although SEC24B mRNA levels remain constant.

claim: SEC24A/B are balanced in a cytoplasmic pool distinct from SEC24C/D.
source: These data imply that SEC24A/B are balanced in a cytoplasmic pool distinct from SEC24C/D.
evidence: SEC24B protein levels increase when SEC24A is absent, while mRNA levels remain constant.

claim: The data raise the possibility of extensive heterogeneity among COPII vesicles and their function in cargo selection and export, determined at least in part by SEC24 paralog composition.
source: Taken together, our data raise the possibility of extensive heterogeneity among COPII vesicles and their function in cargo selection and export, determined at least in part by SEC24 paralog composition.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence showing cargo-specific dependencies on SEC24 paralogs.

claim: Intrinsic selectivity of cargos by SEC24s presumably relies on specific protein-protein interactions.
source: Intrinsic selectivity of cargos by SEC24s presumably relies on specific protein-protein interactions (Lee et al., 2004; Zanetti et al., 2011).

claim: Trans-membrane proteins including SEC22, Syntaxin 5, APP1, and VANGL2, could preferentially interact with some but not all SEC24 paralogs for differential recruitment to the COPII vesicle.
source: Trans-membrane proteins including SEC22, Syntaxin 5, APP1, and VANGL2, could preferentially interact with some but not all SEC24 paralogs for differential recruitment to the COPII vesicle (Mossessova et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Mancias and Goldberg, 2008; Merte et al., 2010).

claim: The cargo receptor LMAN1 interacts equally with all four SEC24 paralogs.
source: In contrast, the cargo receptor LMAN1 interacts equally with all four SEC24 paralogs (Mancias and Goldberg, 2007; Wendeler et al., 2007).

claim: Structural studies have revealed distinct cargo binding sites among SEC24 paralogs that recognize different sorting signals in specific trans-membrane cargos.
source: Structural studies have revealed distinct cargo binding sites among SEC24 paralogs that recognize different sorting signals in specific trans-membrane cargos (Mancias and Goldberg, 2008).

claim: The 'bulk flow' model proposes that soluble cargos exit the ER by default without selection.
source: The 'bulk flow' model proposes that soluble cargos exit the ER by default without selection (Wieland et al., 1987; Martinez-Menarguez et al., 1999; Warren and Mellman, 1999; Thor et al., 2009), and would therefore predict that alterations of overall SEC24 abundance would proportionally affect secretion of all soluble cargos.

claim: The selective dependence of PCSK9 on SEC24A (and to a lesser extent on SEC24B), is inconsistent with the bulk flow model.
source: The selective dependence of PCSK9 on SEC24A (and to a lesser extent on SEC24B), is inconsistent with this model.
evidence: PCSK9 shows specific dependence on SEC24A/B, not all SEC24 paralogs.

claim: PCSK9 represents the first example of a soluble vertebrate cargo that is differentially regulated by specific interaction with selective components of the COPII machinery.
source: Indeed, PCSK9 represents the first example of a soluble vertebrate cargo that is differentially regulated by specific interaction with selective components of the COPII machinery.
evidence: PCSK9 is a soluble protein showing specific dependence on SEC24A/B.

claim: The specificity of PCSK9 for SEC24A/B might be conferred by a cargo receptor that recruits PCSK9 into COPII vesicles for efficient secretion.
source: This specificity might be conferred by a cargo receptor that recruits PCSK9 into COPII vesicles for efficient secretion, in contrast to the bulk flow of more abundant soluble secretory proteins (Martinez-Menarguez et al., 1999; Warren and Mellman, 1999).
evidence: Proposed hypothesis to explain PCSK9 selectivity.

claim: Yeast α-factor is recruited to COPII vesicles and interacts with SEC24.
source: Yeast α-factor is recruited to COPII vesicles and interacts with SEC24 (Kuehn et al., 1998; Shimoni et al., 2000), likely through the cargo receptor ERV29p (Malkus et al., 2002).

claim: Genetic and biochemical studies have identified the LMAN1/MCFD2 complex as the cargo receptor for the soluble coagulation factors V and VIII in mammals.
source: Genetic and biochemical studies have identified the LMAN1/MCFD2 complex as the cargo receptor for the soluble coagulation factors V and VIII in mammals (Nichols et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2003, 2005; Khoriaty et al., 2012).

claim: TANGO1 localized to ER exit sites facilitates loading of bulky cargos such as collagen VII.
source: Additionally, TANGO1 localized to ER exit sites facilitates loading of bulky cargos such as collagen VII (Saito et al., 2009, 2011).

claim: The existence of a PCSK9 ER cargo receptor has been proposed.
source: The existence of a PCSK9 ER cargo receptor has been proposed (Nassoury et al., 2007), but its identity has been unclear.

claim: COPII vesicles coated by SEC24C/D might exclude selected soluble cargos such as PCSK9.
source: Alternatively, COPII vesicles coated by SEC24C/D might exclude selected soluble cargos such as PCSK9.

claim: Additional cytosolic factor may also contribute to the selectivity among SEC24 paralogs as observed in the case of VANGL2 sorting.
source: Additional cytosolic factor may also contribute to the selectivity among SEC24 paralogs as observed in the case of VANGL2 sorting (Merte et al., 2010).

claim: The findings suggest the potential for considerable heterogeneity in the COPII machinery, enabling the accommodation of diverse cargos.
source: Taken together with the broad range of specific phenotypes observed for human and murine mutations in the genes for individual COPII components, our findings suggest the potential for considerable heterogeneity in the COPII machinery, enabling the accommodation of diverse cargos.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence showing cargo-specific dependencies on COPII components.

claim: Complete deficiency for SEC24B or SEC24A in mice is compatible with embryonic development or survival to adulthood, respectively.
source: Although complete deficiency for SEC24B or SEC24A in mice is compatible with embryonic development or survival to adulthood, respectively, no human patients have yet been identified with genetic deficiencies in any of the four SEC24 paralogous genes.

claim: No human patients have yet been identified with genetic deficiencies in any of the four SEC24 paralogous genes.
source: Although complete deficiency for SEC24B or SEC24A in mice is compatible with embryonic development or survival to adulthood, respectively, no human patients have yet been identified with genetic deficiencies in any of the four SEC24 paralogous genes.

claim: The SEC24A-deficient phenotype suggests a potential role for genetic variation at the SEC24A locus in the control of plasma cholesterol in humans.
source: The SEC24A-deficient phenotype suggests a potential role for genetic variation at the SEC24A locus in the control of plasma cholesterol in humans, a key determinant of risk for myocardial infarction and stroke.
evidence: Extrapolation from mouse phenotype to potential human relevance.

claim: Genome-wide association studies for plasma lipid phenotypes have not identified a significant contribution from common genetic variants in the SEC24A gene.
source: Although genome-wide association studies for plasma lipid phenotypes have not identified a significant contribution from common genetic variants in the SEC24A gene (Teslovich et al., 2010), a role for rare alleles at this locus cannot be excluded.

claim: A role for rare alleles at the SEC24A locus in plasma cholesterol control cannot be excluded.
source: Although genome-wide association studies for plasma lipid phenotypes have not identified a significant contribution from common genetic variants in the SEC24A gene (Teslovich et al., 2010), a role for rare alleles at this locus cannot be excluded.
evidence: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

claim: Complete deficiency of SEC24A, even in the presence of haplo-insufficiency of SEC24B, is compatible with survival and normal development in the mouse.
source: Complete deficiency of SEC24A, even in the presence of haplo-insufficiency of SEC24B, is compatible with survival and normal development in the mouse, suggesting that pharmacologic inhibition of hepatic SEC24A expression/function to achieve reduction in plasma cholesterol may be well tolerated as a potential approach to inhibit PCSK9 scretion.
evidence: Genetic crosses showing viability of Sec24agt/gtSec24b+/- mice.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of hepatic SEC24A expression/function to achieve reduction in plasma cholesterol may be well tolerated as a potential approach to inhibit PCSK9 secretion.
source: Complete deficiency of SEC24A, even in the presence of haplo-insufficiency of SEC24B, is compatible with survival and normal development in the mouse, suggesting that pharmacologic inhibition of hepatic SEC24A expression/function to achieve reduction in plasma cholesterol may be well tolerated as a potential approach to inhibit PCSK9 scretion.
evidence: Extrapolation from mouse phenotype to potential therapeutic application.
